dsc:5.translation_en: Cardamom. The best is the kind brought from Commagene, Armenia, and the Bosporus; it also grows in India and Arabia. Choose the kind that is hard to break, full, and closed, since what is not like this is overripe, and choose what strikes the nose with its smell and is sharp and somewhat bitter to the taste. Its power is warming. Taken with water it helps epileptics, coughers, sufferers from sciatica and paralysis, ruptures, spasms, colic, and it expels the broad intestinal worm. Taken with wine it helps kidney ailments, difficulty urinating, scorpion stings, and all venomous bites. A drachma taken with the bark of laurel root breaks stones. Used as a fumigation from below it destroys embryos, and rubbed on with vinegar it removes mange. It is also used in perfume-stabilizing mixtures.

dsc:16.translation_en: Schoinos. One kind grows in Libya, another in Arabia, and another in the region called Nabataea, which is the strongest. The Arabian kind ranks second; some call it Babylonian and others teuchitis. The Libyan kind is useless. Choose it fresh, fiery-red, rich in flowers, purplish when split and fine-textured, smelling of roses when rubbed in the hands, and biting the tongue with some heat. The flower, reeds, and root are used. It has a warming, digestive, softening, opening, diuretic, emmenagogue, wind-dispersing, mildly astringent power, though it can weigh on the head. The flower is useful in drinks for spitting blood and for pains of the stomach, lung, liver, and kidneys, and it is mixed into antidotes. The root is more astringent, so it is given to unsettled stomachs, dropsical patients, and those with spasms, with an equal amount of pepper, a drachma by weight, for several days. Its decoction is suitable as a sitz bath for inflammations around the womb.

dsc:17.translation_en: Aromatic calamus grows in India. The best is tawny, densely jointed, and breaks into many splinters; the inside of the reed is full of whitish cobweb-like fibers, and when chewed it is sticky, astringent, and somewhat sharp. Drunk, it can promote urination. For this reason it is boiled with couch-grass or celery seed and drunk for dropsy, kidney trouble, strangury, and ruptures. Drunk or applied, it brings on menstruation. As a fumigation, either by itself or with turpentine resin, with the smoke drawn through a tube into the mouth, it treats coughs. It is also boiled for women's sitz baths, and it is mixed into plasters and incense for fragrance.

dsc:18.translation_en: Balsam. The tree is seen to be about the size of lycium or pyracantha, with leaves like rue, but much whiter and more evergreen. It grows only in Judaea, in a certain valley, and differs in roughness, height, and slenderness. The thin, hairlike part of the shrub is called easy-to-harvest, perhaps because, being slender, it can be cut easily. The so-called opobalsam is tapped in the heat under the Dog Star by cutting the tree with iron claws. Only a little juice flows, so that each year no more than six or seven choes are gathered, and in that place its weight is sold for double in silver. Good juice is fresh, strong and pure in smell, not acrid, easy to dissolve, smooth, astringent, and moderately biting to the tongue. It is adulterated in many ways: some mix in ointments such as terebinth, cyprinum, mastic oil, lily oil, balaninum, metopion, honey, wax-salve of myrtle, or very liquid cyprinum. Such adulteration is easy to detect. Pure juice, when dropped onto wool and washed out, makes no stain or mark; adulterated juice remains. Dropped into milk, the pure juice curdles it, while the adulterated does not. Poured into milk or water, the pure juice quickly disperses and makes it milky; the adulterated floats like oil, curling and spreading in star-like patterns. Even pure juice becomes worse with age as it thickens. Those who think that pure juice first sinks in water and then rises undispersed are mistaken. The wood called xylobalsam is approved when fresh, slender-twigged, reddish-yellow, fragrant, and faintly smelling of opobalsam. Of the fruit, since it too is necessary in use, choose what is yellow, full, large, heavy, biting and burning in taste, and faintly smelling of opobalsam. A seed brought from Petra, like the seed of hypericum, is used to adulterate the fruit; recognize it because it is larger, hollow, weak, and peppery in taste. The juice has the most active power and is very warming. It clears what darkens the pupils, treats chills around the womb when applied with rose cerate, draws down afterbirth and embryos, disperses chills when rubbed on, and cleans foul ulcers. Drunk, it is digestive and diuretic; it suits those with shortness of breath, those who have drunk aconite with milk, and those bitten by wild animals. It is mixed into pain-relieving plasters, emollients, and antidotes. In general the juice of balsam is strongest, the fruit second, and the wood weakest. The fruit, when drunk, is suitable for pleurisy, pneumonia, coughs, sciatica, epilepsy, dizziness, orthopnea, colic, difficulty urinating, and wild-animal bites; it is also useful in women's fumigations and, boiled, in sitz baths, opening the womb and drawing moisture. The wood has the same powers as the fruit, but weaker. Boiled in water and drunk, it helps indigestion, colic, venomous bites, and spasms, promotes urination, and with dry iris is suitable for head wounds; it also removes scales. It is mixed into the astringent ingredients of perfumes.

dsc:63.translation_en: Myrrh is the tear of a tree that grows in Arabia, like the Egyptian acacia. When the tree is cut, the tear flows down onto mats laid beneath it, while some hardens around the trunk. One kind is called lowland myrrh, oily, from which stacte is obtained by pressing. Another, called Gabirea, is very oily, grows in good rich places, and yields much stacte. The Troglodytic kind ranks first, named from the country that produces it; it is greenish, biting, and clear. Another thin kind is counted after the Troglodytic; it is soft like bdellium, somewhat rank in smell, and grows in sunny places. The so-called kausalis is overripe, black, and glossy. The worst of all is called ergasime: brittle, lacking oil, sharp in appearance and power. The kind called Minaean is rejected. Press-cakes are made from these: from the oily kinds they are fragrant and oily, but from the dry kinds they are without oil, not fragrant, and weak because oil has been added for remolding. Myrrh is adulterated with gum soaked in an infusion of myrrh and mixed in. Choose new myrrh, crumbly, light, uniform in color throughout, showing smooth white nail-like streaks inside when broken, in small lumps, bitter, fragrant, sharp, and warming. Heavy myrrh that is pitch-colored is useless. Its power is warming, stupefying, gluing, drying, and astringent. It softens and opens a closed womb and strongly brings on menstruation and embryos when applied with wormwood, lupine infusion, or rue juice. A bean-sized amount is taken as a pill for chronic cough, orthopnea, pain of the side and chest, looseness of the bowels, and dysentery. Taken with pepper and water two hours before an attack, it relieves chills. It restores roughness of the windpipe and hoarseness when held under the tongue and dissolved. It kills intestinal worms and is chewed for bad breath; with liquid alum it is rubbed on for armpit odor. Rinsed with wine and oil it strengthens teeth and gums. Sprinkled on, it joins wounds of the head; with snail flesh it heals crushed ears and exposed bones, and with poppy juice, castoreum, and glaucium it treats suppurating and inflamed ears. With cassia and honey it is applied to pimples; with vinegar it cleanses lichens; with ladanum, wine, and myrtle oil it strengthens hair that is falling out. Applied with a feather inside the nostrils it soothes chronic catarrhs. It fills ulcers in the eyes, cleans white spots and what darkens the pupils, and scours roughness. Soot from it is made like frankincense soot, as will be shown, and is suitable for the same uses.

dsc:64.translation_en: Boeotian myrrh is the cut root of a certain tree that grows in Boeotia. Choose the kind that resembles myrrh in fragrance. Its power is warming, softening, and dispersing, and it is usefully mixed into incenses.
